We prove that an optimizer's optimal strategy in a budgeted setting requires time-multiplexing; for a $k$-dimensional budget constraint, the optimal strategy strictly decomposes into up to $k+1$ distinct phases, with each phase employing a possibly unique mixed strategy (the case of $k=0$ recovers the classic Stackelberg equilibrium where the optimizer repeatedly uses a single mixed strategy). Second, we address the intriguing question of non-manipulability. We prove that when the learner employs a standard Proportional controller (the "P" of the PID-controller) to pace their bids, the optimizer's utility is upper bounded by their objective value in the Budgeted Stackelberg Equilibrium baseline. By bounding the dynamics of the PID controller via a novel analysis, our results establish that this widely used control-theoretic heuristic is actually strategically robust.

Computer Science and Game Theory.title: Learning vs. Optimizing Players in Budgeted Games
Computer Science and Game Theory.summary:
We study repeated general games over $T$ rounds between a utility-maximizing optimizer and a learning agent, where budget constraints couple the players' decisions across rounds. Without budgets, low swap regret simultaneously guarantees the learner sublinear regret and caps the optimizer at its Stackelberg value. Budgets break this picture: adversarial no-regret becomes impossible, so the natural goals are non-manipulability---no adaptive optimizer earns more than $\mathtt{BSE} \cdot T + o(T)$, where $\mathtt{BSE}$ is its Budgeted Stackelberg Equilibrium value---and low stochastic regret when the optimizer plays a fixed mixed strategy.
  We give an efficient, budget-feasible learning algorithm that achieves both goals in every budgeted game: any adaptive optimizer, budgeted or not, earns at most $\mathtt{BSE} \cdot T + O(\sqrt{T})$ in expectation, and if the optimizer plays a fixed mixed strategy on each of a constant number of intervals, the learner has $O(\sqrt{T})$ regret on each such interval. Our learner best responds to forecasts of the optimizer's play that are calibrated in two novel senses, since under budgets the calibration that prevents manipulation no longer yields low stochastic regret. Response calibration, which conditions on the learner's own mixed response by embedding its continuous mixing weight as a step function in $L^2([-1,1])$, prevents manipulation without discretizing responses; dual-weighted Lagrangian calibration ensures low regret. Although low calibration error requires randomized forecasts---distributions over a continuous space that need not have a succinct representation or be directly computable---we construct such forecasts in polynomial time by simulating online gradient ascent.

Computer Science and Game Theory.title: Pareto-optimal Non-Clairvoyant Scheduling with Predictions
Computer Science and Game Theory.summary: We study preemptive single-machine non-clairvoyant scheduling with predictions, where a prediction of the order of the jobs (or of their sizes) is available, and the objective is to minimize the total completion time. An algorithm is $c$-consistent if it is $c$-competitive when the prediction is correct, and $R$-robust if it is $R$-competitive whatever the prediction. Since the introduction of this problem as one of the first examples of learning-augmented algorithms, the best possible trade-off between consistency and robustness has remained open. We determine it exactly for deterministic algorithms. For every $R>2$, we give an $R$-robust algorithm whose consistency is \[ c(R)=R\Big(1-\Big(1-\frac{R+2}{R^2}\Big)^{\frac R{R+2}}\Big), \] and we prove that no deterministic $R$-robust algorithm, with either predicted order or predicted job sizes, has better consistency. In particular, consistency $1+\varepsilon$ is achievable with robustness $\varepsilon^{-1/2}+\frac16+O(\sqrt\varepsilon)$, whereas all previous algorithms required robustness $Θ(1/\varepsilon)$. Our algorithm is greedy: it follows the predicted order as fast as possible, subject to the invariant that the cost paid so far is at most $R$ times the optimum of the instance in which every unfinished job would end immediately. The matching lower bound rests on the observation that every robust deterministic algorithm must satisfy the same invariant along its run on correct predictions. Furthermore, we give a simple randomized algorithm, using predicted sizes, with consistency $1+\varepsilon$ and robustness $(3\varepsilon)^{-1/2}+O(1)$, strictly below the deterministic frontier. The question of determining the Pareto-optimal frontier among randomized algorithms remains open.

Computer Science and Game Theory.title: The Power and Limits of Money Burning in Bilateral Trade
Computer Science and Game Theory.summary:
We study the power of money burning in bilateral trade. In this problem, a seller owns an indivisible item, a buyer would like to acquire it, and each of these two traders has a private value for the item and the values are sampled from independent distributions. We ask whether the traders can benefit from a mechanism that burns money, that is, one that charges the buyer more than it pays the seller, so that neither trader enjoys the difference (money burnt is a loss for the traders). Is it possible that the traders will ever be better off if the trade mechanism can burn money?
  For Bayesian incentive-compatible mechanisms and for deterministic dominant-strategy incentive-compatible (DSIC) mechanisms, it is known that money burning is always a waste and can only hurt the traders. Maybe surprisingly, we show that once a DSIC mechanism can use randomization, money burning can significantly benefit the traders, and the gain of each of them can be arbitrarily large. In contrast, we show that the power of DSIC randomized mechanisms that burn money is still very limited in the sense that they cannot guarantee any constant fraction of the first-best gains-from-trade.

Computer Science and Game Theory.title: Almost-MMS allocations with small agent redundancy
Computer Science and Game Theory.summary:
For a fixed $ε\ge 0$, let $ρ_{ε, n}$ be the maximum value of $ρ_n$ such that, in every allocation instance with $m$ indivisible goods and $(1 + ε)n$ agents, there is a subset of $n$ agents with the following property. The allocation instance restricted to only this subset of $n$ agents has an allocation that gives each agent at least $ρ_n$-fraction of her $n$-maximin share (MMS).
  When $ε> 0$ we refer to $εn$ as the {\em agent redundancy}. The case $ε= 0$ is the standard setting without agent redundancy, and we use $ρ_{0,n}$ and $ρ_n$ interchangeably.
  For allocation instances with additive valuations, % agents, it is known that $\frac{7}{9} \le ρ_n < 1-Ω(\frac{1}{\log^2 n})$ for every $n \ge 2$ (with stronger lower bounds for small $n$). It is an open question whether $ρ_n$ tends to~1 as $n$ grows. We show that with agent redundancy, the answer to this question is positive. That is, for every $ε> 0$, $ρ_{ε, n}$ tends to~1 as $n$ grows. A straightforward corollary of this result is that for every $c > 0$, if the number of items satisfies $m \le (2 - c)n$, then the answer is positive also for $ρ_n$ (with no agent redundancy). Adapting our techniques to a related setting, we also improve a recent result of Ezra and Garbuz, and show that without agent redundancy, there always exists an allocation that gives $n - O(\log^2 n)$ agents their full MMS.

Computer Science and Game Theory.title: On the Power of Determinism in Multi-Item Auctions
Computer Science and Game Theory.summary:
We study the classical multi-item monopoly setting with a single additive buyer and $m$ heterogeneous items whose values are independent but not necessarily identically distributed. We compare the revenue (REV) of the optimal truthful auction, which in general may be randomized or complicated, with the revenues of three simple deterministic auctions: selling all items separately (SREV), selling them as a single grand bundle (BREV), and choosing the better of the two.
  Our technical cornerstone is a general upper bound on the optimal multidimensional revenue, parameterized by freely chosen item-wise caps, and expressed in terms of optimal single-item, Myersonian revenues and basic statistics of the value distributions. We derive this inequality through Lagrangian duality for a nonlinear programming formulation of the worst-case approximation ratio of separate-selling. Combining this inequality with carefully chosen caps and a probabilistic analysis of the resulting terms, we obtain improved approximation guarantees for all three deterministic auctions, both for general independent values and for iid values. Notably, we prove that $REV\le 2.5\max\{SREV,BREV\}$, improving the long-standing $5.2$ factor of Ma and Simchi-Levi and the $6$ factor of Babaioff, Immorlica, Lucier, and Weinberg. We complement this upper bound with a construction establishing a lower bound of $2.19$, improving the bound of $2$ by Rubinstein.
  For two iid items, we determine the exact approximation ratio of selling separately. Our proof constructs tight Lagrangian dual certificates for the aforementioned programming formulation, when item values lie in the grid $\{0,1/K,2/K,\dots,1\}$, for any discretization parameter $K$. Taking $K\to\infty$ yields the tight ratio $1+W(1/e)\approx1.2785$ in the continuous-valued setting, where $W$ is the Lambert-W function, closing the $[1.278,1.368]$ gap left by Hart and Nisan.
Computer Science and Game Theory.comment: Improved the upper bound on REV/max{SREV,BREV} from 3 to 2.5 for independent items, and added a lower bound of 2.19. For iid items, improved the upper bounds on REV/max{SREV,BREV} to 2.15 and on REV/BREV from 4.18 to 2.5. The improved upper bounds use a new capped revenue inequality obtained via a new Lagrangian dual construction

Computer Science and Game Theory.title: Computational Aspects of Distortion
Computer Science and Game Theory.summary: The distortion framework in social choice theory allows quantifying the efficiency of (randomized) selection of an alternative based on the preferences of a set of agents. We make two fundamental contributions to this framework. First, we develop a linear-programming-based algorithm for computing the optimal randomized decision on a given instance, which is simpler and faster than the state-of-the-art solutions. For practitioners who may prefer to deploy a classical decision-making rule over the aforementioned optimal rule, we develop an algorithm based on non-convex quadratic programming for computing the exact distortion of any (and the best) randomized positional scoring rule. For a small number of alternatives, we find that the exact distortion bounds are significantly better than the asymptotic upper bounds established in prior literature and lead to different recommendations on which rules to use. These results rely on a novel characterization of the instances yielding the worst distortion, which may be of independent interest.

Computer Science and Game Theory.title: Logarithmic Regret for Alternating Mirror Descent
Computer Science and Game Theory.summary: Alternating online mirror descent (AltOMD) is a simple learning rule for zero-sum games, which improves upon simultaneous OMD numerically and theoretically. Previous work obtained $O(T^{1/3})$ and $O(T^{1/5})$ regret bounds for AltOMD, by leveraging modified-energy-function-based analyses. However, settling whether AltOMD achieves near-constant regret has remained an open question. In this paper we resolve the question of whether AltOMD achieves near-constant regret in the affirmative. In particular, we show an $O(log(T))$ regret bound on the sum of the players' external regrets for any two-player zero-sum bilinear game with compact convex strategy sets, under mild regularity assumptions on the regularizers. We verify that our assumptions hold for the negative entropy regularizer, thereby obtaining logarithmic regret for the alternating multiplicative weights updates algorithm. The regret bound also yields an $O(log(T)/T)$ duality gap bound for the averaged strategies.

Computer Science and Game Theory.title: Efficient Equilibrium Computation in Colonel Blotto Games
Computer Science and Game Theory.summary: Colonel Blotto is a fundamental resource-allocation game in which two players divide their budgets across battlefields, and the higher allocation on each battlefield wins its value. The problem of computing an equilibrium efficiently has remained unresolved for its classical continuous version with arbitrary budgets and with values that may vary across battlefields but are the same for both players. We give a fully polynomial-time approximation scheme that computes an $\varepsilon$-Nash equilibrium in time polynomial in the input length and $1/\varepsilon$, and nearly linear in the input length for fixed $\varepsilon$. For sufficiently balanced budgets and battlefield values, we also compute exact equilibria in linear time.

Computer Science and Game Theory.title: Tight Analysis of Randomized Truthful Scheduling: An $(m+1)/2$ Lower Bound
Computer Science and Game Theory.summary: The Nisan-Ronen conjecture, a central problem in algorithmic game theory, asserts that no deterministic truthful mechanism for makespan minimization on $m$ unrelated machines can achieve an approximation ratio better than $m$. Christodoulou, Koutsoupias, and Kovács resolved it in 2023, but the optimal approximation ratio achievable by randomized truthful mechanisms remained open. Recently, Anastasiadis, Christodoulou, Koutsoupias, Kovács, and Schecker extended techniques from the deterministic proof to establish a $(3/2-\sqrt{2})(m-1)$ lower bound for universally truthful mechanisms with discrete support and gave a universally truthful mechanism with approximation ratio $m/2+o(m)$. For the broader class of truthful-in-expectation (TIE) mechanisms, however, the gap remained large: the best known upper bound was $(m+5)/2$, while the lower bound was only $2-1/m$. We prove a lower bound of $(m+1)/2$, determining the optimal TIE approximation ratio up to an additive constant as $m/2+Θ(1)$. Our result also improves the leading constant in the lower bound for universally truthful mechanisms from $3/2-\sqrt{2} \approx 0.0858$ to $1/2$. Together with their $m/2+o(m)$ upper bound, our result determines the optimal approximation ratio for universally truthful mechanisms up to lower-order terms.

Computer Science and Game Theory.title: Payoff scaling shapes cooperation in LLM agents across languages
Computer Science and Game Theory.summary: Large language models (LLMs) are increasingly deployed as autonomous agents that negotiate, coordinate, and make decisions on behalf of human users. Understanding how they cooperate is therefore important for AI governance and machine behaviour research. We examine two factors: payoff magnitude and interaction language. Classical game theory predicts that multiplying all payoffs by a positive constant should not change behaviour because the underlying strategic incentives remain unchanged. We test this prediction using five widely adopted commercial LLMs playing an iterated prisoner's dilemma across ten payoff scales and five languages (English, French, Vietnamese, Chinese and Arabic). Contrary to theoretical expectations, changing only the numerical scale of payoffs substantially alters cooperation. Models respond differently, often in opposite directions, meaning that averages across models can conceal important behavioural heterogeneity. Sensitivity to payoff scale also depends strongly on prompt language. Moreover, payoff scale modifies the effects of persona instructions: at sub-unit stakes, where no payoff shown exceeds 1, all five models cooperate more under a selfish than a cooperative persona, whereas Claude and Gemini reverse this pattern at larger scales. These findings show that cooperation measures depend critically on payoff scale and language and should not be treated as fixed model traits.
Computer Science and Game Theory.comment: Accepted in Interface Focus (Royal Society). 57 pages, 17 figures, 25 tables, including supplementary material

Computer Science and Game Theory.title: Sharp Bounds for Truthful-in-Expectation Scheduling
Computer Science and Game Theory.summary: We study randomized mechanisms for scheduling indivisible jobs on $n$ unrelated machines. Each machine is controlled by a selfish agent who privately knows its processing time for each job. A mechanism assigns every job to a machine and makes payments. We require truthfulness in expectation: no agent can increase its expected payment minus its expected processing cost by misreporting, regardless of the other agents' reports. The makespan is the maximum total processing time assigned to a machine; the objective is to minimize its expectation. We prove that the optimal approximation ratio is $(n+1)/2$ for every $n\ge7$, relative to the minimum makespan of an integral assignment. The lower bound holds for every $n$ and allows unrestricted computation and arbitrary correlations among assignments, assuming finite expected payments and a guarantee uniform over all finite job counts. The matching mechanism uses correlated rounding and runs in expected polynomial bit time on rational inputs. These guarantees hold for all finite nonnegative processing times. For two machines, we characterize the optimal approximation ratio exactly as an analytic constant, approximately $1.505995705434$, and give a mechanism attaining it. For three machines the optimal ratio is $2$. For four, five, and six machines we obtain upper bounds of $3$, $105/32$, and $29/8$, respectively, compared with the general lower bound $(n+1)/2$. The proofs for $n\ge7$ do not rely on computer-assisted certificates; the two- and three-machine results use exact rational computer-assisted certificates.

Computer Science and Game Theory.title: Search and Verification for Strategyproof Facility Location on Metric Graphs
Computer Science and Game Theory.summary:
We study automated design of strategyproof (SP) mechanisms for randomized facility location on continuous metric graphs, with the objective of minimizing total distance. We develop methods for computing upper and lower bounds on the optimal approximation ratio achievable by SP mechanisms for a given graph and number of agents.
  For the lower bound, we propose a cost-preserving reduction to a finite domain that yields lower bounds for unrestricted SP mechanisms through linear programming dual certificates.
  For the upper bound, we introduce finite representations of mechanisms, called piecewise-linear attributions (PL attributions), that mix piecewise-linear deterministic mechanisms using affine weights on a triangulation of the report space. We show that for mechanisms represented by PL attributions, checking SP and an approximation guarantee reduces to finitely many quadratic nonnegativity tests over compact polytopes. With exact arithmetic and comparisons, each verification certifies the proposed property or returns locations where it fails. In addition, we introduce a strengthening of the incentive notion called strong strategyproofness. We show that for fixed component mechanisms and regions of a PL attribution, the strong strategyproofness requirement can be expressed by a finite number of linear constraints on the attribution coefficients. Using these theoretical results, we propose a heuristic procedure for computing an upper bound on the approximation ratio.
  We compute certified upper and lower bounds on several metric graphs and numerically evaluate the proposed search procedure.
  Lastly, we show that deterministic SP onto mechanisms on graphs are strongly strategyproof and admit PL attributions. Thus restricting attention to strongly strategyproof mechanisms admitting PL attributions loses no deterministic SP onto mechanisms.

Computer Science and Game Theory.title: Toward Constant-Factor Maximin Share Guarantees for Subadditive Valuations
Computer Science and Game Theory.summary:
For $n$ agents and $m$ indivisible goods, an agent's maximin share (MMS) is the largest minimum bundle value she can obtain by partitioning the goods into $n$ bundles. Constant MMS approximations are known for additive, submodular, or XOS valuations, but whether such a guarantee exists for general subadditive valuations remains open. We advance this question in two directions. For general subadditive valuations, we exponentially improve the guarantee from $Ω(1/\log\log n)$ to $Ω(1/\log^* n)$, where $\log^* n$ is the iterated logarithm. We then seek constant MMS guarantees under additional structure on subadditive valuations by studying $q$-partitioning valuations: every partition of a bundle into at most $q$ groups admits nonnegative group prices that sum to the bundle's value and whose sum on any collection of groups is at most the value of their union. This hierarchy ranges from subadditivity at $q=2$ to XOS for $q\ge m$. We give the first study of MMS in the intermediate classes and prove constant guarantees whenever $q/n$ has a fixed positive lower bound, including $1/6$ for $q\ge n$ and $1/4$ for $q\ge2n$. For XOS valuations, we further improve the universal guarantee from $4/17\approx 0.2353$ to $5/16=0.3125$.
  For subadditive valuations, we prove a bidding amplification theorem that gives an exponential bound on each agent's probability of receiving less than half her MMS, while satisfying her budget in every outcome. For $q$-partitioning valuations, we give a scalar criterion that converts bounds on the value lost from disjoint deletions within a bundle into bounds on potential losses, even when an agent contributes zero below the target bundle value. For XOS valuations, we prove a reservation theorem that selects goods for integral assignment together with auxiliary additive valuations and accounts for the loss in rounding.

Computer Science and Game Theory.title: Project Submission Games in Participatory Budgeting
Computer Science and Game Theory.summary: We introduce the framework of project submission games, capturing the behavior of project proposers in participatory budgeting (and multiwinner elections). Here, each proposer submits a subset of project proposals, aiming at maximizing the total cost of those that get funded. We focus on finding conditions under which pure Nash equilibria (NE) exist in our games, and on the complexity of checking whether they exist. We also seek algorithms for computing best responses for the proposers

Computer Science and Game Theory.title: Fair Division with Binary Valuations: Characterizations
Computer Science and Game Theory.summary: We consider the fair allocation of indivisible goods with binary valuations. In this setting, the maximum Nash welfare rule, the leximin rule, and all additive welfarist rules with a strictly concave function coincide. We show that for any number of agents, this rule is the only rule that satisfies envy-freeness up to one good, strategyproofness, neutrality, minimal completeness, and invariance under disapproving unassigned goods (IDU). Moreover, we present an alternative characterization for two agents, where we replace IDU with non-redundancy and resource-monotonicity. In both characterizations, all axioms are necessary.
Computer Science and Game Theory.comment: Appears in the 19th International Symposium on Algorithmic Game Theory (SAGT), 2026

Computer Science and Game Theory.title: Linear Equivalence of Full Weight Spectrum Cyclic Orbit Codes
Computer Science and Game Theory.summary: We determine the linear-equivalence classes within the two families of full weight spectrum one-orbit cyclic subspace codes. This solves the second open problem posed by Castello, Polverino and Zullo [J. Combin. Theory Ser. A 212 (2025) 106005]. For the first family, the criterion is a fractional linear transformation over $\F_q$ followed by a power of $q$-Frobenius. For the second family, it is an affine transformation over $\F_{q^2}$ together with a power of $q$-Frobenius. We use polynomial spaces over finite fields, the linear-isometry theorem for cyclic orbit codes, and trace duality. The arguments include parameters belonging to proper subfields of the ambient field.

Computer Science and Game Theory.title: The Complexity of Continuous Contract Design over Polymatroids
Computer Science and Game Theory.summary: We study optimal contracts when an agent allocates continuous effort subject to polymatroid capacity constraints. Effort produces a linear expected reward and incurs a cost. With binary outcomes and limited liability, the principal chooses a single reward share. For linear costs, an optimal contract can be computed in polynomial time. For quadratic costs, the agent has a unique best response computable by polynomially many submodular minimizations, yet optimizing the principal's share is NP-hard even for explicitly represented cut-based rank functions. With $n$ activities, the best-response path can have $2^{n-O(\log n)}$ breakpoints even when each reward coefficient and each rank value is an integer representable in $O(n\log n)$ bits. The construction also answers a question of Allman, Lo, and McCormick on polynomial bit length for source-sink monotone two-parameter minimum cuts. Despite this complexity, an optimal contract for quadratic costs always exists with a share of at most $1/2$. Consequently, $O(1/\varepsilon)$ best-response computations suffice for a $(1-\varepsilon)$-approximation. For rational quadratic costs on explicitly described rational polytopes containing zero, this gives a fully polynomial-time approximation scheme. More generally, a share of at most $1/p$ suffices for continuous convex costs homogeneous of degree $p>1$, on any compact convex action set containing zero. For general convex costs with an exact value and bounded-subgradient oracle, we obtain an oracle approximation scheme using approximate best responses and a supplied lower bound on positive welfare.
Computer Science and Game Theory.comment: 89 pages, 6 figures. The Lean 4 formalization is at https://github.com/philippwarode/contract-design-polymatroids-lean

Computer Science and Game Theory.title: Exploring the Tractability Frontier of Hylland-Zeckhauser Models
Computer Science and Game Theory.summary:
The Hylland-Zeckhauser (HZ) mechanism provides a market-based approach to one-sided matching, making efficient equilibrium computation central to its implementation. Under bi-valued utilities, it admits a strongly polynomial-time algorithm [VY], whereas with four values per buyer, the problem is PPAD-hard under inverse polynomial approximation [CCPY]. To understand the tractability boundary, we study two extensions of the bi-valued case: a third linear utility value and separable concave utilities with two common slopes.
  For every fixed rational $a\in(0,1)$, we prove that computing a normalized additive $\varepsilon_{*}(a)/N$-equilibrium in an $N$-buyer HZ market is PPAD-complete for some constant $\varepsilon_{*}(a)>0$, even when all utilities belong to the same prescribed set $\{0,a,1\}$. This resolves the main question left open by [VY, CCPY]: whether three utility values already suffice for PPAD-hardness. Assuming the PCP-for-PPAD conjecture, we strengthen the above-stated result to constant additive-error hardness.
  For the concave extension, we compute an exact equilibrium in strongly polynomial time with two marginal utility slopes common across goods for each buyer and arbitrary rational buyer-good breakpoints. With three common marginal slopes, suitable breakpoints encode the three valued linear case, yielding PPAD-hardness.
  Thus, our paper identifies two thresholds separating tractable and intractable cases of HZ models with utility functions specified by utility values or marginal slopes. In both cases, the tractability threshold lies between two and three.

Computer Science and Game Theory.title: Domination-Avoiding Learning Agents Cannot Collude
Computer Science and Game Theory.summary: An influential paper of Calvano et al. empirically demonstrated that Q-learning agents spontaneously collude when placed as sellers that compete on prices in a natural market model. More recent results of Fish et al. empirically demonstrated that similar collusion happens with commercial LLMs. We formally prove that such collusion can also happen with external-regret-minimizing agents. We identify a very general class of agents, which we term Domination-Avoiding agents, that provably do not collude in such markets. This class contains all Mean-Based agents and all internal-regret-minimizing agents, as well as others such as Multiplicative-Weight agents with variable learning rate and contextual variants thereof. More generally we show that, in any game, this class of agents is guaranteed to jointly learn to almost never play strategies that are eliminated by repeated elimination of purely dominated strategies.
Computer Science and Game Theory.comment: 27 pages, 1 figure. Accepted to NeurIPS 2026 (Spotlight). Camera-ready version

Computer Science and Game Theory.title: Best-of-Many-Worlds MMS Allocation for Chores with Sublinear Disposals
Computer Science and Game Theory.summary: We study randomized allocations (lotteries) of indivisible chores under additive costs and introduce the notion of MMS1, which requires each agent's bundle to satisfy the maximin share (MMS) bound after the removal of at most one chore. Our main result establishes that every instance admits an ex-ante proportional lottery in whose support every allocation is MMS1 and all but $o(n)$ agents satisfy MMS. Consequently, every realized allocation can be made MMS by disposing of at most $o(n)$ chores. The proposed framework further achieves ex-ante proportionality alongside ex-post $4/3$-MMS, $o(n)$-AMMS, or $1$-out-of-$d$ MMS for $d=(1-o(1))n$. These guarantees substantially improve upon state-of-the-art bounds for MMS allocation for chores with disposal or subsidy, best-of-both-worlds fairness, approximate AMMS, and ordinal MMS approximations.

Computer Science and Game Theory.title: Robust Aggregation of Quantile Statistics: from Median to Interval
Computer Science and Game Theory.summary:
Quantile-based summaries, such as prediction intervals and medians, are commonly used in economic forecasting, climate science, and public health. For highly skewed samples, experimental evidence suggests that estimates of the mean can be biased toward the median, whereas estimates of the median are relatively accurate. This motivates aggregating explicitly elicited quantiles rather than reported means.
  We study robust aggregation of quantile reports for bounded outcomes under squared loss, minimizing worst-case regret relative to an omniscient Bayesian aggregator who knows the information structure and observes all private signals. Without restrictions on the information structure, no rule improves on the constant forecast at the range midpoint in worst-case regret. We therefore consider weak substitutes, a diminishing-returns condition on the value of information, and characterize optimal aggregation rules under this condition.
  For central prediction intervals with common nominal coverage $α$, the optimal rule, which we call regularized simple average for prediction intervals, shrinks the average reported interval midpoint toward the range midpoint, with a weight determined by $α$ and the number $n$ of experts. This optimal rule strictly improves on the constant baseline in worst-case regret when $α<1/\sqrt{n}$; at or above this threshold, the constant rule is optimal. The optimal worst-case regret is minimized at a unique interior coverage level, revealing a nonmonotonic relationship between coverage and aggregation performance. For median reports, regularized simple average for medians similarly shrinks the average reported median toward the range midpoint, assigning weight $1/n$ to the reported average and strictly improving on the constant baseline in worst-case regret for every finite $n\ge2$.

Computer Science and Game Theory.title: Bankruptcy Rules for Strategic Agents
Computer Science and Game Theory.summary:
Bankruptcy rules are rules for dividing an insufficient estate among people with different claims. Existing rules assume that the claims are publicly known. When this is not the case, claimants have a strong incentive to claim more than they are due, as bankruptcy rules give larger allocations to claimants with larger claims. A remedy often used by legal systems is to make over-reporting costly by requiring evidence and imposing penalties. But this remedy also increases the legal expenses of proving true claims, which might result in under-reporting. Encouraging true reporting requires fine-tuning of the legal costs.
  This paper incorporates the costs of supporting both true and false claims into the bankruptcy model. Claimants incur costs for the true and false parts of their claims, with false claims costing at least as much per unit as true claims. The goal is to set cost rates that induce claimants to report their true entitlements, neither more nor less. Whether this is possible depends on the allocation rule. The proportional and constrained equal awards rules cannot guarantee truthfulness at any positive true-claim cost rate; the same holds for constrained equal losses with at least three claimants.
  For $N\ge2$ claimants, the rule TAL-1/N from the parameterized Talmud family induces truthfulness exactly when the true-claim cost rate is at most 1/N and the false-claim cost rate is at least 1-1/N. This rule is optimal in the sense that its truthful cost region contains that of every piecewise smooth allocation rule: it gives the legal system the maximum possible flexibility in setting the legal costs. For two claimants, TAL-1/2 (aka Contested Garment rule) uniquely attains this optimal region.

Computer Science and Game Theory.title: Existence of the Core in Approval-Based Committee Elections
Computer Science and Game Theory.summary:
We resolve the central open question in the theory of approval-based committee elections: we prove that the core is always non-empty. This means that there always exists a committee for which no coalition of voters can deviate to an alternative committee of proportional size that every member strictly prefers. This property was introduced by Aziz et al. (2017) to capture proportional representation and coalitional stability, but no known algorithm achieved it except up to a constant approximation factor or in special cases.
  Our approach begins by strengthening the core to core+, which requires the committee to be robust even to fractional deviations. Using LP duality, this property can equivalently be defined in terms of a payment-based certificate under which no losing candidate gathers too much support. We then define a voting rule that chooses a committee admitting a certificate that maximizes a novel harmonic entropy objective function, which rewards balanced payment distributions. We show that the payment system associated with an optimal committee certifies that the committee satisfies core+, establishing existence. The same is true for local optima, which allows us to design a polynomial-time algorithm computing a core+ committee.
Computer Science and Game Theory.comment: 43 pages, with a completely rewritten exposition of the argument

Computer Science and Game Theory.title: Logarithmic Comparison-Query Complexity for EF1 Allocations
Computer Science and Game Theory.summary: We study the comparison-query complexity of computing allocations that are envy-free up to one item (EF1) for $n$ agents with heterogeneous additive preferences over $m$ indivisible items. In this model, the algorithm may only query which of two bundles an agent prefers, without ever observing numerical valuations or costs. Prior work established $O(\log m)$ query bounds for at most three agents, leaving open whether query complexity logarithmic in $m$ is achievable for every fixed $n \ge 4$. We resolve this open question in the affirmative: for every fixed $n\ge2$, we design algorithms that compute EF1 allocations using $O(\log m)$ comparison queries, matching the known $Ω(\log m)$ lower bound. Our results hold for both chores with nonnegative costs and goods with nonnegative valuations.

Computer Science and Game Theory.title: Designing AI-Mediated Communication in Teams
Computer Science and Game Theory.summary: AI assistants increasingly participate in work that requires employees to exchange information and coordinate decisions. We study how a firm should design this communication when workers' interests conflict with each other's and the firm's. Two workers privately know local conditions and their preferred responses, while the assistant knows aggregate project conditions. The firm discloses project information before workers report and choose their own actions. Transparency improves adaptation but can undermine truthful preference reporting. When workers agree with the firm on the productive direction, coarsening project information under weak coordination can preserve useful preference reporting at a cost in forecast precision. Under strong coordination, the firm instead prefers full project disclosure and factual reports, because preference information induces costly accommodation of private objectives. Under weak coordination, a firm-optimal policy can leave workers worse off than direct exchange; requiring their acceptance can call for further coarsening. Releasing project context after reports can sustain factual communication that early release would prevent. With separate delivery decisions that cannot be revised jointly, endogenous forwarding weakly improves firm-preferred performance over unchanged forwarding and strictly improves it in some environments. Numerical comparisons show that full initial disclosure captures most gains in the aligned environments considered, while further design has greater value when workers can favor opposing directions. The results distinguish the credibility of employees' reports from their organizational value and show how disclosure timing affects both.

Computer Science and Game Theory.title: Settling the Complexity of Hylland--Zeckhauser Equilibria
Computer Science and Game Theory.summary: The Hylland--Zeckhauser (HZ) mechanism is a foundational framework for allocating indivisible goods in one-sided matching markets via lotteries supported by competitive prices and equal artificial budgets. We resolve the exact computational complexity of the HZ scheme by proving that computing an exact HZ equilibrium is FIXP-complete, thereby settling a conjecture of Vazirani and Yannakakis. Notably, this hardness persists even when computing the equilibrium allocation alone. We establish our hardness result via a reduction that encodes quadratic fixed-point equations into a reciprocal variational inequality. On the algorithmic side, we present a deterministic polynomial-time approximation algorithm that achieves an additive error of $0.0755211 + δ$ for any $δ> 0$, significantly improving upon the previous $1/e$ guarantee.

Computer Science and Game Theory.title: Cutting Down the Tower: Single-Exponential Envy-Free Cake Cutting
Computer Science and Game Theory.summary:
Envy-free cake cutting is a central problem in fair division with a striking divide between existence and computation. Classical topology guarantees that envy-free allocations exist, yet finding one efficiently (in the Robertson-Webb query model) has resisted decades of work. The seminal work by Aziz and Mackenzie established the existence of a bounded protocol for every $n$, but its query bound is $n^{n^{n^{n^{n^n}}}}$. Subsequently, Sokolov modified their protocol and sharpened its analysis, obtaining a bound of $n^{8n^2(1+o(1))}$ queries, the best deterministic upper bound known before this work. In contrast, the general lower bound, due to Procaccia, is merely $Ω(n^2)$.
  We close much of this gap with a deterministic protocol using $n^{O(1)}2^n$ queries, the first single-exponential bound for general valuations. Like Aziz and Mackenzie, we repeatedly allocate cake without envy until some agents can leave with their pieces, guaranteed not to envy anyone who stays, even if a staying agent receives all the remaining cake. To reach this state, Aziz and Mackenzie generate $n^{n^{n^n}}$ partial allocations so that enough of them can be redistributed without conflict. Instead, we show that only polynomially many partial allocations suffice. Our key idea is to ``prune'' scarce allocations upfront: if only a few allocations can help a certain pair of agents, we discard them and handle that pair another way, leaving plenty of allocations for every remaining pair so each gets a distinct one. As a result, we make only polynomially many calls to Aziz and Mackenzie's subroutines, and this gives us our $n^{O(1)}2^n$ bound.

Computer Science and Game Theory.title: Stable Voting Rules on the Edge of Optimal Metric Distortion
Computer Science and Game Theory.summary: We prove the existence of a randomized voting rule with metric distortion at most $2.1248$, within $0.013$ of the lower bound of $2.11264$. Our rule comes from a generalization of \emph{stable $k$-lotteries} developed in the context of committee selection. In contrast to prior work, our rule samples from a single distribution derived from a zero-sum game, without mixing between voting rules. Our result also gives sharp distortion bounds for stable $k$-lotteries. In particular we show that stable $2$-lotteries have distortion $7/3$, despite only relying on aggregate preferences over triples of candidates, and that stable $2$-lotteries are optimal in this class of voting rules.

Computer Science and Game Theory.title: Coercive at the equilibrium, monotone nowhere: exact convergence certificates for learning in first-price auctions
Computer Science and Game Theory.summary: The Bayes-Nash equilibria of an auction are the solutions of a variational inequality, and for standard auctions its operator fails every monotonicity notion, so the theory of monotone operators is unavailable to learning in auctions. We show what replaces monotonicity for the first-price auction: a certificate that is strong but local. For uniform values the single-population operator has an exact closed form and an exact Minty identity at the equilibrium; for two bidders its Gateaux derivative there is $L^2$-coercive with best constant exactly one in every piecewise-linear bid space with $m$ pieces, while the Minty inequality holds only on a ball whose radius decays like $m^{-5/2}$. The decay is exact: $m^{5/2}$ times the radius converges to $1/(8 \cdot 3^{1/4})$, and the worst perturbations converge to an alternating geometric profile with ratio $-(2-\sqrt{3})$. Refinement shrinks the ball, not the constant; independent learners see the same constant. For a general prior and bidder count there are two certificates, at the true equilibrium and at the equilibrium of the finite-dimensional bid space a learning algorithm runs in. The first is an explicit weight $w_F$, positive for every log-concave prior, equal to the second exactly for the value distributions $F(v)=v^a$. Otherwise the learners' certificate differs by knot masses, because the discretized equilibrium's slopes oscillate with a law proved for two and three bidders, and for four under a computer-verified bottom layer. The limit of the learners' certificate is proved in closed form, a function of the prior alone, and characterizes positivity: positive uniformly in $m$ in the limit exactly when that minimum is positive, with a known rate; for one prior at every $m$ by interval arithmetic. For more bidders the limit is conjectured. The exact identities and leading-order inequalities are machine-checked in Lean.

Computer Science and Game Theory.title: Balanced Fair Division and Generalized Kneser Graphs
Computer Science and Game Theory.summary:
We study indivisible goods allocated to two prescribed nonempty groups whose members have arbitrary monotone valuations. We guarantee balanced envy-freeness up to one good (EF1) for at most five agents and up to two goods (EF2) for at most nine, for any number of goods. Bundle sizes differ by at most one. The EF1 threshold is sharp: every split of six agents can fail. EF2 improves the previous five-agent guarantee.
  Via the connection of Kyropoulou, Suksompong, and Voudouris, these guarantees follow from chromatic bounds for $\mathrm{KG}(2n,n,r)$, whose vertices are $n$-subsets of a $2n$-set, adjacent when their intersection has size less than $r$. We prove its chromatic number is six for $r=2$, $n\ge2$, resolving Jafari and Alipour's conjecture, and at least ten for $r=3$, $n\ge4$, improving the previous lower bound of six; the known upper bound is fourteen.
  We show that the standard box-complex $\mathbb{Z}_2$-index bound yields exactly five and nine for $n\ge3$ and $n\ge5$, respectively. To exceed these bounds, we exploit restrictions on maps induced by colorings: a proper five- or nine-coloring must induce a nonzero homology map, yet local constraints force all generators, supported on pentagon or rook configurations, to map to zero. The ten-color proof compares integral and fractional common centers using a sharp rounding theorem for five subset constraints.
  A linear-time retraction from the full allocation graph onto balanced layers adds cardinality balance to known nonlinear discrepancy guarantees. For each fixed removal allowance in the guaranteed-existence range, finding a balanced fair allocation or an explicit monotonicity violation from valuation circuits is polynomial-time equivalent to finding a monochromatic edge in a circuit-specified coloring of the corresponding graph. The reverse reduction produces normalized monotone binary valuations using ordinary circuits.

Computer Science and Game Theory.title: On the Complexity of Exact Autobidding Equilibria
Computer Science and Game Theory.summary: Autobidding equilibria link advertisers' value multipliers or participation probabilities through aggregate budget and return-on-investment (ROI) constraints. We establish the exact computational complexity of finding these equilibria across several canonical settings: exact equilibrium computation is $\mathsf{FIXP}$-complete for second-price ROI pacing, budget- or ROI-constrained generalized second-price (GSP) sponsored shopping, and second-price throttling. Furthermore, approximating the equilibrium control vector in distance to a true equilibrium is $\mathsf{FIXP}_{a}$-complete when the target accuracy is provided as input.

Computer Science and Game Theory.title: The Power of Recruiting the Smaller Side: Two Additional Traders Suffice in Two-Sided Markets
Computer Science and Game Theory.summary:
We study Bulow-Klemperer-style competition complexity in two-sided double auctions with $m$ unit-demand buyers drawn i.i.d. from $F_B$ and $n$ unit-supply sellers drawn i.i.d. from $F_S$. When $m \ge n$ and buyer valuations first-order stochastically dominate seller costs ($F_B \succeq_{\mathrm{FSD}} F_S$), we prove that recruiting just two additional sellers enables Seller Trade Reduction (STR), a prior-independent mechanism, to achieve expected Gains From Trade (GFT) at least the first-best GFT of the original market; symmetrically, when $m \le n$, Buyer Trade Reduction suffices with two additional buyers. This resolves open questions of Babaioff, Goldner, and Gonczarowski (SODA 2020) and Cai, Liaw, Mehta, and Zhao (STOC 2024). Moreover, this uniform bound is optimal: already for $m = n = 1$, no prior-independent mechanism (deterministic or randomized) that is dominant-strategy incentive-compatible (DSIC), individually rational (IR), and weakly budget-balanced (WBB) matches the first-best GFT with one additional seller.
  We further extend our characterization to $r$-dominance ($F_B \succeq_r F_S$), where $r \in (0, 1]$ and $1 - F_B(x) \ge r(1 - F_S(x))$ for all $x \in \mathbb{R}$ (recovering $F_B \succeq_{\mathrm{FSD}} F_S$ at $r = 1$). When $m \ge n \ge 1$, $c = \lceil 1/r \rceil + 1$ additional sellers suffice for STR to match or exceed the first-best GFT, while every prior-independent DSIC, IR, and WBB mechanism requires at least $\max(2, \lceil 1/r \rceil - 1)$ additional sellers even for $m = n = 1$, pinning down the optimal bound to within two traders. Finally, this $Θ(1/r)$ bound cannot be asymptotically improved even by recruiting on both sides: for $r < 1/64$ and $m = n = \lceil 2/(5r) \rceil$, every prior-independent DSIC, IR, and WBB mechanism requires $c \ge \lceil 1/(64r) \rceil = Ω(1/r)$ additional traders per side.

Computer Science and Game Theory.title: Single-or-Sample: Online Fair Allocation for Combinatorial Agents
Computer Science and Game Theory.summary:
We study the fair allocation of $m$ indivisible goods among $n$ heterogeneous agents arriving online, under maximin share (MMS) fairness. The key challenge lies in making allocation decisions in an adversarial setting without knowing future agents' valuations. No guarantees were known prior to our work in adversarial settings.
  Our main positive result is an online allocation algorithm for submodular agents that with probability at least $0.4$ guarantees a $1/24$-approximation to MMS to all agents simultaneously. Our algorithm intersperses a greedy-style adaptive sampling-without-replacement protocol with single-good reduction rounds. For XOS valuations, we adapt this single-or-sample approach to guarantee a $c$-MMS for all agents simultaneously with probability $1-O(c)$ for any parameter $c\in O(1/\log n)$. A key technical contribution of our work is in establishing Chernoff-style tail bounds on item allocation events for this adaptive sampling process despite strong positive correlations among the items, a result that may be of independent interest.
  The approximation versus success probability tradeoffs achieved by our algorithms are asymptotically tight. We show that even for binary additive valuations, no randomized algorithm can ensure $c$-MMS to all agents with probability exceeding $(1-c^2/5)$, for any $c\in (0,1]$. For XOS valuations, stronger lower bounds hold: no randomized algorithm can ensure $c$-MMS to all agents with probability exceeding $(1-c/3)$, for any $c\in (0,1]$. Furthermore, no algorithm can achieve $ω(1/\log \log n)$-MMS with any constant probability. All our lower bounds hold even for simple binary instances whose MMS values and MMS partitions can be computed in linear time.

Computer Science and Game Theory.title: Arbitrarily Slow Polynomial Convergence of Fictitious Play
Computer Science and Game Theory.summary: We show that fictitious play can converge at arbitrarily slow polynomial rates in two-player zero-sum games. For every integer $k \ge 2$, we construct a payoff matrix with $(k+1)^2 - 5$ actions per player for which the duality gap of the empirical strategies decays as $Θ(t^{-1/k})$ after $t$ steps. The family starts from the standard rock-paper-scissors matrix, with each higher-order game constructed recursively from the preceding one. After a prescribed common initial action, every subsequent best response under fictitious play is unique. For $k \ge 3$, these games give counterexamples to Karlin's conjectured $O(t^{-1/2})$ convergence rate, and they extend the recent $Θ(t^{-1/3})$ construction of Wang (2025) to arbitrarily slow polynomial rates.

Computer Science and Game Theory.title: On the Role of Geometry in Solving Variational Inequalities
Computer Science and Game Theory.summary:
The geometry of constraints in variational inequalities (VIs) plays a central role in applications ranging from resource allocation and equilibrium computation to constrained optimization. Yet, its effect on computational complexity has received surprisingly little attention beyond special cases. We examine this question when the constraint set is an $\ell_p$ ball. This family of problems encompasses two of the most extensively studied classes of problems in algorithmic game theory: symmetric bimatrix games for $p = 1$ and multi-player polymatrix games for $p = \infty$. Both of these problems are known to be PPAD-complete even for affine operators.
  We establish a comprehensive complexity landscape for VIs over $\ell_p$ balls across the full range $p\in[1,\infty]$. First, for any $p\neq 2$, we show that finding an inverse-polynomial approximate VI solution is PPAD-complete even for affine operators. In contrast, for $p=2$, we give a polynomial-time algorithm for affine VIs, extending a classic result of Ye (1992) beyond symmetric operators. On the other hand, once the operator becomes quadratic, we establish PPAD-completeness even at inverse polynomial precision.
  From a technical standpoint, we develop a new toolkit for exploiting the geometry of the constraint set and the structure of the operator to characterize the complexity of equilibrium and optimization problems, which is of independent interest.

Computer Science and Game Theory.title: Dynamic Pooling and Regional Participation in Deceased-Donor Organ Allocation
Computer Science and Game Theory.summary: Moving from geographically fragmented to pooled waiting lists in deceased-donor organ transplantation can improve efficiency, but it raises concerns about regional fairness and participation incentives. This paper studies Pareto gains from such transitions in a multi-class queueing model with impatient agents, perishable items, and a tractable homogeneous compatibility friction. In contrast to standard approaches that emphasize static match quality or overlook regional incentives in dynamic contexts, this analysis identifies dynamic risk pooling as the primary source of Pareto improvements for regions. Pooling reduces organ waste resulting from stochastic supply-demand fluctuations, temporal mismatches, and random compatibility outcomes. Although this dynamic surplus theoretically enables Pareto improvements, a purely utilitarian policy that treats all patients equally across regions often fails to achieve these improvements when regions are asymmetric. In these situations, utilitarian redistribution removes an excessive number of organs from high-supply regions and violates their participation constraints. To address this conflict, it is demonstrated that the set of achievable utilities can be represented by mixtures of static priority index policies. Building on this structure, the Constrained Pareto Frontier Search (CPFS) is proposed as a polynomial-time procedure that computes an approximately optimal allocation policy with arbitrarily small participation-constraint violations. The results indicate that, by adjusting priority indices to ensure redistribution remains within the gains from pooled supply, demand, and compatibility risk, policymakers can achieve global efficiency while maintaining local participation incentives.

Information Retrieval.title: Darwin Family: MRI-Trust-Weighted Evolutionary Merging for Training-Free Scaling of Language-Model Reasoning
Information Retrieval.summary: We present Darwin Family, a framework for training-free evolutionary merging of large language models via gradient-free weight-space recombination. We ask whether frontier-level reasoning performance can be improved without additional training, by reorganizing latent capabilities already encoded in existing checkpoints. Darwin introduces three key ideas: (i) a 14-dimensional adaptive merge genome enabling fine-grained component- and block-level recombination; (ii) MRI-Trust Fusion, which adaptively balances diagnostic layer-importance signals with evolutionary search through a learnable trust parameter; and (iii) an Architecture Mapper that enables cross-architecture breeding between heterogeneous model families. Empirically, the flagship Darwin-27B-Opus achieves 86.9% on GPQA Diamond, ranking #6 among 1,252 evaluated models, and outperforming its fully trained foundation model without any gradient-based training. Across scales from 4B to 35B parameters, Darwin models consistently improve over their parents, support recursive multi-generation evolution, and enable a training-free evolutionary merge that combines Transformer- and Mamba-based components. Together, the Darwin Family demonstrates that diagnostic-guided evolutionary merging is a practical and reproducible alternative to costly post-training pipelines for reasoning-centric language models.
Information Retrieval.comment: arXiv admin note: This submission has been withdrawn because it does not meet arXiv's research content quality standards

Information Retrieval.title: Neural networks and games
Information Retrieval.summary: Hopfield neural networks and noncooperative games provide seemingly different approaches to understanding how collective outcomes emerge from local interactions. In a neural network, individual units adjust their states according to local signals; in a game, players choose actions to maximise individual payoffs. I establish an exact equivalence between symmetric binary Hopfield networks and binary-action games that admit a quadratic potential. The equivalence identifies stable network configurations with pure-strategy Nash equilibria, and asynchronous neural updating with best-response dynamics. More broadly, the storage and retrieval of memories in neural networks correspond, respectively, to the design and selection of equilibria in games.

Information Retrieval.title: Learning Behaviorally Relevant Dynamics in Multimodal Neural Recordings
Information Retrieval.summary: Multimodal neural data can enable a more complete understanding of brain dynamics underlying behavior. Modalities such as spiking activity, local field potentials (LFPs), and behavior capture diverse spatiotemporal aspects of brain processes, yet prior neural-behavioral models that separate sources of variability rely on a single neural modality. By leveraging these complementary strengths, multimodal neural fusion can provide a unified, rich representation of brain-behavior processes and address the limitations of single-modality analyses. Here we develop BREM-NET, a nonlinear multimodal dynamical model that integrates behavior with multiple neural modalities having distinct statistical characteristics and temporal resolutions. BREM-NET performs multimodal neural fusion during inference while separating behaviorally relevant and residual neural dynamics via a structured learning framework. In a public multimodal non-human primate dataset with simultaneous spiking and local field potential recordings during a 2D reaching task, BREM-NET separates these two types of dynamics and learns them more accurately, as reflected in better behavior decoding, better neural prediction, and stronger latent alignment with behavior, and it retains these capabilities when neural modalities are asynchronous or suffer dropouts, which are major challenges in real-world recordings. This framework provides a new tool for studying behaviorally relevant neural computations across spatiotemporal scales of brain activity.

Information Retrieval.title: Solving the Nonlinear Westervelt Equation in Ultrasound Propagation Using Physics-Informed Neural Networks
Information Retrieval.summary: Modeling the nonlinear acoustic wave propagation in biological tissues needs accuracy, especially in ultrasound imaging and therapeutic applications. The 1D Westervelt equation, \( p_{xx} - p_{tt} + γ\, p_{ttt} + η\,(p^{2})_{tt}=0, \) could be used to describe a finite-amplitude ultrasound propagation in these tissues. This equation accounts for nonlinearity, \(η\), and attenuation, \(γ\). To solve this equation, we observe that traditional solvers may struggle to do so correctly. This is due to the difficulties arising from the nonlinear nature of the equation. We solve the equation by defining three synthetic cases - linear (\(η=0.001\), \(γ=10^{-6}\)), shock-dominated (\(η=0.02\), \(γ=10^{-6}\)), and dissipation-dominated (\(η=0.01\), \(γ=5\times10^{-4}\)) - and using Physics-Informed Neural Networks (PINNs) to showcase the solution. A sinusoidal activation function is used to capture the oscillatory behavior of the problem. The results of our study, with PDE residual converging to at least \(10^{-6}\), boundary condition loss to \(10^{-5}\), and the PINN loss converging to \(10^{-5}\) for each case at \(30,000\) epochs, show that \(γ\) scales the rate of amplitude decay, while \(η\) governs frequency-dependent phase speeds.
Information Retrieval.comment: 17 pages, 21 figures

Information Retrieval.title: Diffusion models for eye-gaze trajectory generation using position and velocity representations
Information Retrieval.summary: Eye-tracking data are expensive to collect, requiring specialized hardware and controlled laboratory conditions, and difficult to share due to privacy regulations, which together limit the quantity and diversity of gaze data available for research. We investigate unconditional gaze generation using diffusion models in position and component-wise velocity representations. The models are trained and evaluated on eight-second visual-search trajectories from 28 participants, using a split of 23 training participants and five held-out validation participants, with three training seeds. Evaluation includes kinematic distributions, trajectory geometry, event statistics, and a temporal Wasserstein GAN with gradient penalty as a learned comparator. Across eight position-derived features, mean Jensen-Shannon divergence is $0.016 \pm 0.004$ for the position model and $0.037 \pm 0.002$ for the velocity model, with standard deviations calculated across training seeds. These scores do not establish that representation choice caused the difference. A separate comparison using the same evaluation method shows that the ordering of the models varies across training seeds. The position model also produces smaller feature discrepancies than a kinematic Markov baseline. Differences in saccade counts between real and generated data depend strongly on the velocity threshold used to detect events. The results provide quantitative reference measurements for unconditional gaze generation on this visual-search task and show how evaluation choices affect conclusions about generated gaze.
Information Retrieval.comment: 13 pages, 9 figures

Information Retrieval.title: Correlations Are Ruining Your Gradient Descent
Information Retrieval.summary: Natural gradient descent, and the preconditioned optimizers which have followed from it, correct gradient descent by estimating curvature and applying its inverse to the gradient. For any single layer of a deep neural network, this correction can be shown to approximately separate into two factors: one which accounts for correlations in the gradient signal, and one which accounts for correlations in the data arriving at that layer. Herein we show that this second factor can be expressed as a change of basis rather than of curvature and, considered thus, it can be removed from the optimizer entirely and placed within the network itself. Specifically, we show that, once forward weights are corrected, right-sided natural gradient descent can be implemented in a form which has three exactly equivalent forms: a gradient preconditioner, a decorrelating linear transform in the forward pass, or a set of recurrent dynamics in which all updates are Hebbian and rely only upon locally available signals. The (recurrent) decorrelation method we discover aligns closely with proposed methods for inhibitory learning and homeostatic plasticity in the brain. Notably, our transform requires no matrix inverse, no matrix decomposition, and no information beyond that which is available at an individual synapse. It can therefore be applied in distributed and physically constrained systems, including neuromorphic hardware and nervous systems, where existing preconditioners cannot. We demonstrate its effectiveness empirically in convolutional and residual network models while significantly improving a range of approximate biologically plausible methods for credit assignment.
Information Retrieval.comment: 26 pages, 6 figures

Information Retrieval.title: Subspace Node Pruning
Information Retrieval.summary: Node pruning is the art of removing computational units such as neurons, filters, attention heads, or even entire layers to significantly reduce inference time while retaining network performance. In this work, we show that a broad family of importance measures, from activation-based to Fisher-based, share a common quadratic form. Through a lower-triangular change of basis, this form yields a pruning subspace in which entire nodes can be removed while the impact of the lost units is simultaneously recovered via linear least squares. Furthermore, the importance measures within our subspace are decoupled and additive through an orthogonalization of the layer activations, allowing multi-node pruning within layers without interference between importance scores. Our method, Subspace Node Pruning (SNP), outperforms the compared baselines on VGG-16 and ResNet-50 on ImageNet. On OPT-125M and LLaMA-2 7B, SNP matches the state-of-the-art LLM Surgeon at a 40-shot schedule and outperforms it whenever fewer shots are used, all without any retraining after pruning.
Information Retrieval.comment: 18 pages, 6 figures, 5 tables

Information Retrieval.title: Hardware-Aware Model Inversion in Memristive Spiking Neural Networks
Information Retrieval.summary:
Hardware-accelerated spiking neural networks (SNNs) implemented on memristive crossbar arrays offer significant gains in energy efficiency, while device variability and analog noise are sometimes assumed to hinder information extraction. However, whether these hardware effects improve, preserve, or degrade privacy after deployment remains largely unexplored. Therefore, we ask whether model-inversion leakage characterized on an SNN remains representative after the same model is mapped to a non-ideal memristive substrate, and how hardware non-idealities and reliability faults affecting synapses, neuron thresholds, and spike processing reshape that leakage. To study this problem, we introduce Spiking Domain Model Inversion (SDMI), an inversion method that combines Expectation over Transformation (EOT) with surrogate gradients to optimize inputs through stochastic analog behavior and non-differentiable spiking dynamics. We use SDMI consistently across the SNN model, its memristive SNN, and the same memristive SNN under additional hardware perturbations.
  Across four datasets, reconstruction leakage does not vary monotonically with model accuracy or hardware variability. At comparable accuracy levels, neuron-threshold perturbations increase reconstruction fidelity, measured by SSIM, by up to 51.8%, whereas spike-level perturbations primarily degrade utility without consistently improving reconstruction. Weight noise, in contrast, reduces leakage under the same inversion procedure. These results show that hardware variability is not inherently privacy-preserving: model inversion leakage in memristive SNNs depends on the hardware state and cannot be inferred from model accuracy alone.
Information Retrieval.comment: 15 pages, 8 figures

Information Retrieval.title: Cultural Evolution Drives the Emergence of Conventions in Neural Emergent Communication
Information Retrieval.summary: Recent studies of language evolution with neural agents often use models where agents can either speak or listen, where there are only two agents in the population, or where agents can share internal representations. These choices prevent the study of how language emerges through cultural evolution, i.e. through the cumulative adaptation of individual behaviours to fit the communicative needs of the community. We tackle this issue with a new model that trains populations of bi-directional neural agents in a fully distributed fashion to solve a referential game. We demonstrate the effectiveness of this approach on multiple image datasets and show that it is able to scale to large populations. We also show that more conventional languages are easier to learn, providing a direct advantage for cultural transmission. Overall, this work provides a novel approach to neural emergent communication that opens up new directions for evolutionary linguistics.

Information Retrieval.title: Refined CMA-ES for CEC 2026 Bound-Constrained Single-Objective Optimization
Information Retrieval.summary: We present a simplified and parameter-adjusted variant of CMA-ES designed for the CEC 2026 Bound-Constrained Single-Objective Optimization competition. Unlike typical algorithmic developments that increase complexity by adding mechanisms, Refined CMA-ES systematically removes components that do not improve performance, such as the flat-land escape, while retaining standard features that provide measurable benefits. Adjusting key parameters (population size and initial step-size) yields substantial gains, outperforming the baseline CMA-ES and several state-of-the-art competitors. The paper highlights the practical relevance of individual CMA-ES components under the CEC 2026 ranking, which equally weights solution accuracy and convergence speed, demonstrating that simplification combined with improved parameter settings can lead to superior performance.
Information Retrieval.comment: 4 pages pre-print, accepted to IEEE CEC 2026 as a full paper, published in IEEE CEC 2026 Proceedings

Information Retrieval.title: FiTS: Interpretable Spiking Neurons via Frequency Selectivity and Temporal Shaping
Information Retrieval.summary: Spiking Neural Networks (SNNs) are a promising framework for event-driven temporal processing. Prior work has improved temporal modeling through richer neuron dynamics and network-level mechanisms such as recurrence and delays, but it remains unclear how individual spiking neurons should specialize within a network. In this work, we introduce FiTS, a spiking neuron that factorizes temporal computation within each neuron into Frequency Selectivity (FS) and Temporal Shaping (TS). The FS module parameterizes each neuron's target frequency as the maximizer of its subthreshold magnitude response, while the TS module reshapes when frequency components contribute to membrane voltage accumulation through group-delay modulation. On auditory benchmarks where frequency selectivity and timing are central to the input structure, FiTS consistently improves over a plain Leaky Integrate-and-Fire (LIF) baseline in simple feedforward SNNs without recurrence or network-level delays, while remaining competitive with strong temporal SNN baselines. Beyond accuracy, the learned target frequencies and group-delay shifts provide interpretable neuron-level summaries of the frequency and timing organization learned within the network. Our code is available at https://github.com/kaistmm/FiTS.
Information Retrieval.comment: Accepted at NeurIPS 2026 (Spotlight). Code is released at https://github.com/kaistmm/FiTS

Information Retrieval.title: Knowledge-Guided Memetic Algorithm for Capacitated Arc Routing Problems with Time-Dependent Service Costs
Information Retrieval.summary: The capacitated arc routing problem with time-dependent service costs (CARPTDSC) is a challenging combinatorial optimization problem that arises from real-world applications. CARPTDSC has two main challenges in reducing computational time. First, it is an NP-hard problem. Second, the time-dependent service costs of tasks require frequent evaluations during the search process, significantly increasing the computational burden. These challenges make it difficult for existing algorithms to perform efficient searches, often resulting in limited efficiency. To address these issues, this paper proposes a knowledge-guided memetic algorithm with golden section search and negatively correlated search (KGMA-GN), where two knowledge-guided strategies are introduced to improve efficiency. First, a knowledge-guided initialization strategy (KGIS) is proposed to generate high-quality initial solutions to speed up convergence. Second, a knowledge-guided small-step-size local search strategy (KGSLSS) is proposed to filter out invalid moves, thereby reducing unnecessary evaluations. Experimental results on five benchmark test sets, including both small- and larger-scale instances, demonstrate that KGMA-GN achieves higher search efficiency than the state-of-the-art methods. Moreover, the ablation study further confirms that the knowledge-guided local search operators in KGSLSS can significantly reduce runtime compared to traditional operators, especially for the knowledge-guided swap operator, which achieves more than a tenfold improvement in speed.
Information Retrieval.comment: Accepted for publication in IEEE Transactions on Emerging Topics in Computational Intelligence. Updated to the accepted version with the IEEE copyright notice

Machine Learning.title: Algorithmic Principles For Multiclass Learning Are Hard To Come By: Limits of Regularization and Proper Learning
Machine Learning.summary:
Two of the most fundamental questions in statistical learning theory are the following: which prediction problems are learnable, and how should they be learned? For the former, elegant answers often take the form of combinatorial dimensions. The latter question, however, has proved considerably more elusive: all known general-purpose multiclass learners rely on intricate orientations of exponentially large one-inclusion structures, and familiar algorithmic principles such as proper learning and regularization remain poorly understood. Motivated by prior work, we ask whether learning reduces to proper learning---possibly over a larger hypothesis class---and whether proper or improper multiclass learning can ultimately be captured by suitable regularizers.
  Our primary results answer both questions negatively, resolving three open problems from prior work. First, we exhibit a learnable multiclass problem that cannot be embedded in any properly learnable class, meaning learning cannot be reduced to proper learning by enlarging the hypothesis class. Second, we demonstrate that proper learning can require training error and characterize this phenomenon precisely: every properly learnable class admits a proper learner making $o(m)$ errors on samples of size $m$, but every prescribed sublinear scale $a_m=o(m)$ is necessary for some properly learnable problem. Third, regularization is not a general learner: we exhibit a properly learnable class that cannot be learned by any Structural Risk Minimization (SRM) learner, and a learnable class that cannot be learned by any local regularizer. We complement these impossibility results with a positive theory that gives two sufficient conditions for SRM learnability and characterizes SRM representability through integrability of revealed preferences.

Machine Learning.title: Generative Modeling for Cascading Extremes via Autoregressive Transformers
Machine Learning.summary: Extreme events often occur sequentially, from earthquake-tsunami cascades to successive extreme losses in financial markets. We introduce an extremal token representation that encodes multivariate observations as a categorical sequence. A quiet token records the absence of threshold exceedances; otherwise, the token identifies the exceeding component with the largest marginal probability-scale score. The representation is invariant to componentwise strictly increasing transformations. It preserves the identity and temporal ordering of dominant exceedances but discards their magnitudes and the identities of nondominant simultaneous exceedances. A decoder-only transformer estimates the history-dependent next-token kernel on this representation, and recursive sampling generates future token sequences from the induced joint predictive law. We amortize our generative model by pretraining across simulated process families with varying parameters and dependence persistence. Next-token predictions are evaluated against exact conditional probabilities for held-out categorical processes and particle filter references for heavy-tailed vector autoregressive processes. Applied to ten-second returns for five semiconductor stocks, the pretrained model supports zero-shot transfer, while a few epochs of adaptation improve agreement between observed and generated token frequencies and transition patterns. These results support task-specific tokenization and simulation-based pretraining for modeling which dimensions dominate multivariate extremes.

Machine Learning.title: Balance-Guided Forest for Causal Effect Estimation
Machine Learning.summary: Covariate balancing is widely used for estimating causal effects in observational studies. A central challenge is determining which covariate features should be balanced. Forest-kernel balancing provides a data-driven way to learn informative balancing features. Existing forest-kernel balancing methods first learn a tree-based representation and then construct balancing weights. However, this procedure creates a mismatch, as limited tree capacity may be spent on features that are already well represented. We propose Balance-Guided Forest (BGF), which uses the current balancing weights to guide subsequent tree construction. BGF grows trees using a novel splitting score that combines residual imbalance with an outcome contrast, favoring splits that separate outcome-relevant regions where imbalance remains. This couples representation learning with covariate balancing rather than treating balancing as a downstream step. We establish an oracle-type bound that links the iterative construction to weighting error and causal bias. Simulations exhibit improvements in causal estimation relative to existing forest-kernel approaches. Real-data applications illustrate the practical behavior of BGF across observational studies.

Machine Learning.title: From Type to Token: Petri Nets, Individual Token Philosophy, and Individualized Causal Effects
Machine Learning.summary:
Structural Causal Models and Bayesian Networks are the dominant framework for representing causal relations. They are fundamentally type-level formalisms since their estimands, Average Treatment Effects and Conditional Average Treatment Effects, are properties of distributions over populations, not of individual units. When treatment effects exhibit unbounded heterogeneity, these estimands collapse. What persists is the structural, token-level core of causation.
  We argue that Petri Nets under the Individual Token Philosophy are the natural representation of these token-level causal structures. We develop a formal translation from Bayesian Networks to Petri Nets, providing a two-layer account of individualized causality. The PN layer provides a structural representation of causal mechanisms that does not rest on distributional assumptions. In turn, a conformal prediction layer quantifies causal effects with finite-sample coverage guarantees. Together they constitute a complete account of individual causal effects.

Machine Learning.title: Decoupling Distance and Networks: Hybrid Graph Attention-Geostatistical Methods for Spatio-temporal Risk Mapping
Machine Learning.summary: Accurate spatial prediction and rigorous uncertainty quantification are central to modern spatial epidemiology and environmental risk analysis.
